screens.title: Conditionals, Loops, and Jinja2 Templating
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn three interlocking skills that make Ansible playbooks adaptive and maintainable. First, conditionals let you control when a task runs by expressing logic with familiar operators, membership tests, and careful parentheses for precedence. Second, loops let you repeat tasks across lists and dictionaries while understanding how the special item variable exposes keys and values. Third, Jinja2 templates take facts and variables and render configuration files that vary per host. Together these features let your automation respond to different operating systems, inventories, and runtime facts without duplicate playbooks. For example, you will see patterns that run user-creation only on Red Hat systems, iterate over a list of user dictionaries to create accounts with specific shells, and generate a motd file that shows the current date and host interfaces. We will also cover common pitfalls: overly complex when clauses, misunderstanding item structure in loops, and templating secrets unsafely. By the end you will be able to write conditional tasks that are idempotent, loop cleanly over structured data, and craft templates that include filters and tests to produce robust configuration.

screens.title: Advanced when conditions
screens.narratorSegment: A when condition decides whether a task runs by evaluating a Jinja2 expression that resolves to true or false. At its simplest you compare a variable to a value, but real playbooks often need compound logic. Use and, or, and not to combine tests, and prefer explicit parentheses to make intent clear. Membership tests like in and not in are essential when you want a task to run only for hosts in a group or when a value appears in a list. For example, a task should run when the host is in a maintenance group and a flag variable is defined and true. To keep conditions readable, consider precomputing complex logic in vars or set_fact and then using a short when expression referencing that var. One common mistake is writing ambiguous expressions without parentheses; Python-like precedence can produce surprising results. Another pitfall is relying on undefined variables: a bare reference can cause errors, so guard with is defined or use default. Finally, prefer separate tasks with focused when clauses when a single when becomes unwieldy. Try this short pattern in your head: set a helper var that captures the intent, then use when: helper_var to keep tasks clear and debuggable. How could you simplify a long expression into a descriptive variable?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Advanced when conditions
Definition and rules
  • Use and, or, not, ==, !=, <, >, <=, >= for comparisons and logic.
  • Use in / not in for membership tests against lists or strings.
  • Wrap complex logic in parentheses to ensure correct evaluation order.
Common mistake
Chaining multiple operators without parentheses can produce unexpected outcomes; prefer a precomputed var to capture intent and improving readability.
Example pattern
- name: Set condition helper
  set_fact:
    should_manage_users: "{{ (inventory_hostname in groups['webservers']) and (feature_flag is defined and feature_flag) }}"

- name: Manage users when helper true
  ansible.builtin.user:
    name: '{{ item.name }}'
    state: '{{ item.state | default("present") }}'
  loop: '{{ users }}'
  when: should_manage_users
This pattern keeps the when clause short and the intent named, which helps debugging and reuse.
Key Takeaway

Prefer short when clauses that refer to well-named vars computed earlier; guard undefined variables with is defined or default.

screens.title: Loop strategies and evolution
screens.narratorSegment: Loops let you repeat tasks for many items without duplicating task definitions. Historically Ansible used constructs like with_items and with_dict; modern playbooks use loop because it's consistent and powerful. loop accepts lists, the output of other modules, or the result of filters such as dict2items. When looping over a simple list, item becomes the element. When looping over a list of dictionaries, item becomes a dictionary and you can access fields like item. name. For dictionaries, convert them to items with dict2items to iterate key/value pairs predictably. A typical workflow begins by deciding the data shape you need, normalizing it—often using set_fact or filters—and then using loop. If you need backward compatibility, with_items behaves similarly for simple lists, but avoid mixing old and new styles. A common pitfall is assuming item is always a string; when working with dicts, test with a debug task to inspect item. In practice you will often collect users as a list of dicts, loop to create accounts, and join groups with the join filter. This process keeps your tasks general and reusable across inventories.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Loop strategies and evolution
Step-by-step loop process
  1. Decide the data shape: list of values, list of dicts, or a dict.
  2. Normalize a dict into items with dict2items when needed.
  3. Use loop to iterate; inspect item with debug to confirm structure.
  4. Access item fields directly when iterating dictionaries, e.g., item.name.
Pro tip
Use loop_control.label to provide a readable label in task output when item is complex.
Example converting a dict
- name: Iterate firewall rules stored in a dict
  set_fact:
    fw_rules: "{{ my_rules_dict | dict2items }}"

- name: Apply firewall rules
  ansible.builtin.firewalld:
    service: "{{ item.key }}"
    state: "{{ item.value.state }}"
  loop: "{{ fw_rules }}"
dict2items produces a list of key/value objects so item.key and item.value are available consistently.
Key Takeaway

Prefer loop and convert dictionaries to items so item access stays predictable and safe.

When removing users, set state to absent and ensure any dependent tasks handle that change idempotently. This walkthrough includes a compact playbook snippet you can drop into your lab and adapt to your inventory. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Looping over a list of user dictionaries
Explanation
When items are dictionaries, access fields directly. Use filters to supply reasonable defaults and to convert lists to module-friendly formats.
Checklist before running:
  • Debug item to confirm structure if unsure.
  • Use default for optional fields like shell or groups.
  • Prefer append: yes when adding groups to avoid overwrite.
Key Takeaway

Always normalize and inspect data shape; handle missing keys with default and format list fields for the module's expectations.

Example playbook snippet
- name: Manage multiple users
  ansible.builtin.user:
    name: "{{ item.name }}"
    state: "{{ item.state | default('present') }}"
    groups: "{{ item.groups | default([]) | join(',') }}"
    shell: "{{ item.shell | default('/bin/bash') }}"
  loop:
    - { name: 'devuser1', groups: ['developers', 'sudo'], state: 'present', shell: '/bin/zsh' }
    - { name: 'opsuser', groups: ['ops', 'sudo'], state: 'present' }
    - { name: 'guestuser', groups: [], state: 'absent' }
Add a preceding debug task if you want to inspect item before applying changes: use debug: var=item or debug: msg='{{ item }}'.

screens.title: Iterating dictionaries: dict2items and with_dict
screens.narratorSegment: Dictionaries are common inventory structures for configuration. To loop predictably over a mapping's key/value pairs use dict2items, which converts a dict into a list of objects with key and value fields. This makes item. key and item. value available in your loop and avoids ambiguous behavior. While with_dict is a legacy construct that implicitly iterates key/value pairs, dict2items combined with loop is the clearer modern approach. Use set_fact to produce the list from the dict so the same normalized data shape is available across tasks. When iterating nested values, be explicit about what you're indexing to avoid KeyError-like templating problems. A frequent mistake is assuming iteration order; if order matters, explicitly convert the dict into a sorted list of items using the sort filter. Another gotcha is nested dictionaries where value itself may be a mapping; in that case iterate over item. value with another loop or use subkeys in templates. Finally, prefer small, testable conversions and debug output to verify assumptions before applying system-changing tasks. Iterating dictionaries: dict2items and with_dict means normalize a dict to a list with dict2items and loop for clear item.key/item.value access; sort when order matters.. In practical terms, turn mappings into iterable lists and avoid surprises. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Iterating dictionaries: dict2items and with_dict
Why normalize a dict
Normalization creates a consistent item structure so subsequent tasks can rely on item.key and item.value. It also enables sorting and filtering before iteration.
When to sort:

If the order of operations matters, convert and sort the list to avoid unpredictable iteration ordering across Python versions or Ansible runs.

Example conversion
- name: Convert mapping to items
  set_fact:
    users_list: "{{ users_map | dict2items }}"

- name: Create users from mapping
  ansible.builtin.user:
    name: "{{ item.key }}"
    state: "{{ item.value.state | default('present') }}"
    groups: "{{ item.value.groups | default([]) | join(',') }}"
  loop: "{{ users_list }}"
This approach uses item.key for the username and item.value for properties, keeping semantics explicit.
Common misconception

Don't assume dict iteration preserves a desired order; if you need stability, convert and sort explicitly before looping.

screens.title: Jinja2 filters and tests
screens.narratorSegment: Jinja2 filters transform variable values in templates and playbooks; tests inspect properties and return true or false. Filters such as default, upper, int, join, to_nice_json, and password_hash allow you to coerce types, format lists, and hash secrets before use. Tests like is defined, is none, and is string let you conditionally include content or choose default values when a variable is missing. A typical robust pattern is to combine both: use is defined to check a value, then apply default if necessary, and finally format it with a filter. This avoids undefined-variable errors at template render time. Another useful filter is to_nice_json, which is great for embedding debug-friendly JSON into files. Be cautious: filters execute during template rendering on the control node, so avoid passing secrets in plain text through logs. When you expect numeric configuration, cast with int to ensure downstream code interprets types correctly. Filters and tests let you keep templates concise while handling variable variability gracefully. Jinja2 filters and tests means use filters to shape output and tests to check properties; combine them to produce predictable templates that handle undefined values gracefully.. In practical terms, transform values and guard templates with filters and tests. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Jinja2 filters and tests
Common filters
  • default: provide fallback values when undefined.
  • join: convert lists to strings for modules requiring comma-separated values.
  • int and upper: cast and format values.
  • to_nice_json: produce readable JSON for debug or files.
Useful tests
  • is defined: guard access to variables that may not be present.
  • is none: detect explicit null values.
  • is string: confirm expected types before formatting.
Template example
{{ "{{ app_port | default(8080) | int }}" }}
This pattern provides a fallback and ensures the value is an integer for configuration files.
Misconception

Assuming filters run on the remote host. Templates render on the control node during the template task, so be mindful of available facts and secrets.

screens.title: Templating with template module and control-node rendering
screens.narratorSegment: The template module renders a Jinja2 template on the control node and then copies the resulting file to the target host. That order matters: templates can only reference variables that are available at render time. If a fact is gathered later on the target machine, it won't be available to a template in the same play unless you gathered those facts earlier or passed them explicitly. Use default and is defined to avoid render-time failures when variables are missing. The motd example in this chapter demonstrates conditional content and loops inside a template: you can include a welcome line that differs when ansible_os_family equals RedHat, and loop over ansible_interfaces to list them. Also apply filters like ansible_date_time. iso8601 for a consistent timestamp. For secrets, avoid rendering raw passwords into files or logs; hash or vault them and limit template exposure in logs. Always test templates with dummy data first and run ansible-playbook --syntax-check to catch templating syntax errors early. Templating with template module and control-node rendering means templates are rendered before transfer; ensure required variables are available and avoid leaking secrets in rendered output or logs.. In practical terms, render dynamic config safely and predictably. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Legacy constructs vs modern usage
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible historically provided with_items and with_dict for simple iteration. While they still work, loop is the recommended single construct that handles lists, dictionaries, and results uniformly. with_items sometimes hid differences in variable expansion, leading to confusing item shapes. With dicts, with_dict provided implicit key/value access but mixing with_dict and loop can confuse readers. The modern approach is to transform a dict with dict2items into a predictable list of objects and then use loop. This produces item. key and item. value explicitly, which improves readability and reduces surprises. When you encounter legacy playbooks, refactor them to loop and dict2items incrementally: first run tests with debug output to confirm behavior, then update task definitions. A practical benefit is consistent loop_control options and uniform behavior when working with register results. Avoid trying to support both patterns in a single task; pick modern loop patterns for clarity and maintainability. screens.title: Common pitfalls and troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: When working with conditionals, loops, and templates you will encounter a few recurring issues. Syntax errors in templates are a frequent cause of failures; run ansible-playbook --syntax-check and ansible-lint before full deployment. Undefined variables during template rendering fail on the control node; protect every optional variable with default or is defined checks. For loops, the most common surprise is mistaken assumptions about item: always inspect with debug: var=item if the loop comes from an unknown source. Another class of problem is over-complex when expressions: if a condition has many operators, split the logic into a set_fact or vars section and use a descriptive name in the when. Finally, be careful with secrets in templates — avoid printing raw passwords, and if a template needs a secret, prefer vault or hashing. For troubleshooting, add debug tasks, run plays in check mode when safe, and log rendered templates to a temporary location for inspection. These steps make debugging faster and avoid unintended changes to systems. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Build dynamic_config.yml and motd.j2
Starter playbook (dynamic_config.yml)
---
- name: Dynamic User and MOTD Configuration
  hosts: all
  become: yes
  vars:
    managed_users:
      - { name: 'devuser1', groups: ['developers', 'sudo'], state: 'present' }
      - { name: 'opsuser', groups: ['ops', 'sudo'], state: 'present' }
      - { name: 'guestuser', groups: [], state: 'absent' }

  tasks:
    - name: Ensure 'developers' group exists
      ansible.builtin.group:
        name: developers
        state: present
      when: ansible_os_family == 'RedHat'

    - name: Manage users based on defined list
      ansible.builtin.user:
        name: "{{ item.name }}"
        state: "{{ item.state }}"
        groups: "{{ item.groups | join(',') }}"
        append: yes
      loop: "{{ managed_users }}"
      when: ansible_os_family == 'RedHat'

    - name: Deploy dynamic Message Of The Day (MOTD)
      ansible.builtin.template:
        src: motd.j2
        dest: /etc/motd
        mode: '0644'
Starter template (templates/motd.j2)
# /etc/motd - Generated by Ansible
---------------------------------------------------
Date: {{ ansible_date_time.iso8601 }}
Hostname: {{ inventory_hostname }}

{% raw %}{% if ansible_os_family == 'RedHat' %}{% endraw %}
Welcome to a Red Hat-based system!
{% raw %}{% else %}{% endraw %}
Welcome to a Linux system!
{% raw %}{% endif %}{% endraw %}

Network Interfaces:
{% raw %}{% for interface in ansible_interfaces %}{% endraw %}
  - {{ interface }}
{% raw %}{% endfor %}{% endraw %}
---------------------------------------------------

Run ansible-playbook -i inventory dynamic_config.yml after verifying inventory hosts, then check /etc/motd and user accounts on the target hosts.

screens.title: Common assessment: service selection by OS family
screens.narratorSegment: A common assessment asks you to manage different services depending on ansible_os_family. The safe, idempotent approach uses separate tasks each guarded by a when clause: one task to ensure httpd is started when ansible_os_family equals RedHat, and another to ensure nginx runs when ansible_os_family equals Debian. This avoids trying to start the wrong service on the wrong host. An alternative is using a Jinja2 expression to choose the service name in a single task. That can work for simple value selection but can lead to attempting to manage the wrong package or service if other variables differ across hosts. When constructing these tasks, prefer the separate-task pattern because it is explicit and easier to debug. For assessment, demonstrate both forms and explain the trade-offs: clarity and idempotence versus compactness. Finally, test with a mixed inventory and validate that the correct service is running on each host, and include a debug task to print the chosen service name when troubleshooting. Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Service selection by OS family
Preferred (explicit) pattern
- name: Ensure httpd is running on RedHat
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: httpd
    state: started
  when: ansible_os_family == 'RedHat'

- name: Ensure nginx is running on Debian
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: nginx
    state: started
  when: ansible_os_family == 'Debian'
This pattern ensures each task only runs where appropriate and avoids accidental management of the wrong service.
Alternative (single task)
- name: Ensure web service is running
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: "{{ 'httpd' if ansible_os_family == 'RedHat' else 'nginx' }}"
    state: started
This is concise but can attempt to manage a service not present on the system if other factors differ. Use with caution and verify package availability first.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn three interlocking skills that make Ansible playbooks adaptive and maintainable. First, conditionals let you control when a task runs by expressing logic with familiar operators, membership tests, and careful parentheses for precedence. Second, loops let you repeat tasks across lists and dictionaries while understanding how the special item variable exposes keys and values. Third, Jinja2 templates take facts and variables and render configuration files that vary per host. Together these features let your automation respond to different operating systems, inventories, and runtime facts without duplicate playbooks. For example, you will see patterns that run user-creation only on Red Hat systems, iterate over a list of user dictionaries to create accounts with specific shells, and generate a motd file that shows the current date and host interfaces. We will also cover common pitfalls: overly complex when clauses, misunderstanding item structure in loops, and templating secrets unsafely. By the end you will be able to write conditional tasks that are idempotent, loop cleanly over structured data, and craft templates that include filters and tests to produce robust configuration.

By the end of this chapter you will be comfortable expressing precise conditions, iterating structured data, and rendering dynamic files with Jinja2. Objective one focuses on advanced when conditions: you'll learn to combine and, or, not, comparison and membership operators, and to use parentheses for clear precedence. Objective two covers loop strategies: you'll use loop for lists and task results, understand legacy constructs like with_items and with_dict, and convert dictionaries to iterable lists with dict2items. Objective three teaches Jinja2 filters and tests so you can transform values, set defaults, and guard against undefined variables in templates. Objective four brings these together in the template module: you'll render configuration files that vary by host facts and safely handle sensitive data. Each objective emphasizes practical patterns, a short example, and a common mistake to avoid so you can apply these skills in real playbooks.

This second objectives screen connects skills to tangible demonstrations. You will demonstrate advanced when conditions by creating tasks that run only for Red Hat-based hosts, combining defined checks and membership tests to avoid accidental execution. For loops, you will author a loop that creates users from a list of dictionaries and remove users using state absent; you will inspect the item structure with debug to verify keys. For templating, you will produce a motd that shows the current date and interface list and uses default to fall back to values when variables are undefined. Finally, you will apply best practices: run ansible-playbook with --syntax-check and use ansible-lint before deployment, avoid embedding raw secrets in templates, and favor precomputed vars for complex conditions to keep tasks readable. Each objective maps to a verification step you can run in a lab: check /etc/motd contents, verify created users, and observe that conditional tasks did not run on non-matching hosts.

A when condition decides whether a task runs by evaluating a Jinja2 expression that resolves to true or false. At its simplest you compare a variable to a value, but real playbooks often need compound logic. Use and, or, and not to combine tests, and prefer explicit parentheses to make intent clear. Membership tests like in and not in are essential when you want a task to run only for hosts in a group or when a value appears in a list. For example, a task should run when the host is in a maintenance group and a flag variable is defined and true. To keep conditions readable, consider precomputing complex logic in vars or set_fact and then using a short when expression referencing that var. One common mistake is writing ambiguous expressions without parentheses; Python-like precedence can produce surprising results. Another pitfall is relying on undefined variables: a bare reference can cause errors, so guard with is defined or use default. Finally, prefer separate tasks with focused when clauses when a single when becomes unwieldy. Try this short pattern in your head: set a helper var that captures the intent, then use when: helper_var to keep tasks clear and debuggable. How could you simplify a long expression into a descriptive variable?

Loops let you repeat tasks for many items without duplicating task definitions. Historically Ansible used constructs like with_items and with_dict; modern playbooks use loop because it's consistent and powerful. loop accepts lists, the output of other modules, or the result of filters such as dict2items. When looping over a simple list, item becomes the element. When looping over a list of dictionaries, item becomes a dictionary and you can access fields like item. name. For dictionaries, convert them to items with dict2items to iterate key/value pairs predictably. A typical workflow begins by deciding the data shape you need, normalizing it—often using set_fact or filters—and then using loop. If you need backward compatibility, with_items behaves similarly for simple lists, but avoid mixing old and new styles. A common pitfall is assuming item is always a string; when working with dicts, test with a debug task to inspect item. In practice you will often collect users as a list of dicts, loop to create accounts, and join groups with the join filter. This process keeps your tasks general and reusable across inventories.

Looping over a list of dictionaries is a common pattern for resource management. When each item is a dictionary, item becomes a mapping that you can index with dot notation. In the provided user example we iterate managed_users where each element includes name, groups, and state. Use default to protect missing fields; for groups, default to an empty list and join to produce the comma-separated string expected by the user module. Append: yes ensures users are added to existing groups rather than replacing them. A practical way to validate your assumptions is to add a debug task that prints item and item. keys to confirm the shape before any state-changing tasks run. A common misconception is that loop always yields strings; it does not. Another pitfall is forgetting to join lists when a module expects a comma-separated string. When removing users, set state to absent and ensure any dependent tasks handle that change idempotently. This walkthrough includes a compact playbook snippet you can drop into your lab and adapt to your inventory. Looping over a list of user dictionaries means when looping over dicts, use item.key access and filters like default and join to avoid runtime errors and unexpected replacements.. In practical terms, create or remove users with item fields and defaults. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Dictionaries are common inventory structures for configuration. To loop predictably over a mapping's key/value pairs use dict2items, which converts a dict into a list of objects with key and value fields. This makes item. key and item. value available in your loop and avoids ambiguous behavior. While with_dict is a legacy construct that implicitly iterates key/value pairs, dict2items combined with loop is the clearer modern approach. Use set_fact to produce the list from the dict so the same normalized data shape is available across tasks. When iterating nested values, be explicit about what you're indexing to avoid KeyError-like templating problems. A frequent mistake is assuming iteration order; if order matters, explicitly convert the dict into a sorted list of items using the sort filter.
